newsitem.title: MALI: Christopher campaigns for democracy on Africa tour.
newsitem.headline: Christopher campaigns for democracy on Africa tour.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher pursued his campaign for democracy in Africa on Tuesday with a scheduled meeting with the reformist soldier who helped end one-party dictatorship in Mali.
Christopher arrived in Mali on Monday at the start of a five-nation Africa tour, saying he would seek support from U.S. allies for new sanctions against Nigeria's military rulers.
He is also using the tour to rally Africans behind the United States in its determination to deny Boutros Boutros-Ghali a second term as U.N. Secretary General.
Officials said Christopher chose Mali to launch his tour as a tribute to its smooth transition from one-party dictatorship to multi-party democracy in a free-market environment.
And to honour the main architect of that change, Christopher was due to meet army commander General Amadou Toumani Toure, whose 1991 coup helped bring down dictator Moussa Traore.
Toure staged the coup amid a popular uprising against Traore, during which loyalist troops killed scores of civilians.

But instead of clinging to power as coupmakers have done elsewhere in Africa, Toure made clear he was serving only as interim president. He allowed elections to be held, used soldiers to ensure an effective process, then stepped aside for elected president Alpha Oumar Konare to take over in 1992.

Officials travelling with Christopher have drawn comparisons between Toure and George Washington, the first U.S. president who played a key role in binding the nation more than 200 years ago into a single whole under a democratic system.
Toure is still at the head of the Malian army but is revered in Africa as a statesman, whose mediation is sought after in trouble spots like Burundi.
He has not declared any intention to seek the presidency in due course but has publicly voiced support for soldiers seeking elected office as long as they first leave the army.

Before touching down in Mali, Christopher said he would seek support from partners to push for sanctions to help the campaign for democracy and human rights in Nigeria, the regional giant he has pointedly avoided on the tour.

"I think we'll be starting a round of consulations with Commonwealth countries and our European allies to see if we can find support for taking further action (against Nigeria)," Christopher told reporters on his plane before landing in Mali.

Citing human rights abuses and corruption, Christopher said Washington "continues to be very troubled by our relationship with Nigeria...as much because of the tremendous potential Nigeria has and the failed promise of Nigeria."

The United States followed its European allies in imposing token sanctions against Nigeria, which angered the international community last November by hanging nine minority activists convicted of murder by a special tribunal.
But like other Western nations, the United States stopped short of imposing an embargo on Nigeria's oil, which human rights campaigners say would be the most effective sanction.

Christopher is also seeking support in Africa for a U.S. bid to replace Boutros-Ghali as U.N. chief. Washington, the biggest contributor to the U.N. budget, insists the Egyptian must be replaced with a more reform-minded secretary general who will steer the world body to meet the challenges of the 21st century.

"Everywhere I go, I'm going to be talking about the importance of Africa coming forward with good candidates for the U.N. secretary generalship," he told reporters aboard his U.S. Air Force jet enroute to Mali.
